unit-phys-graphs.title: Kinematics 1 · Motion Graphs and the Constant-Velocity Lab
unit-phys-graphs.srcName: HW04 Kinematics Graphs and Lab 1: Constant Motion (Drive)
unit-phys-graphs.source: Physics 8, Kinematics — 'HW04 Kinematics Graphs' and 'Lab_Constant Velocity' (Drive)

summary.text: Two pieces of the kinematics unit, both about reading motion off a graph rather than out of a formula. The constant-motion lab: take position and time data for a car, fit a line of best fit, and get a slope, a y-intercept, a percent error and a mathematical expression out of it — then use that expression to predict a distance and to solve backwards for a time. The graphs homework: position-versus-time and velocity-versus-time graphs — which intervals are forward, which backward, which at rest; average velocity against average speed; acceleration segment by segment; displacement as the area under a velocity graph; and matching a position graph to the velocity graph that describes the same motion.

why.text: A graph is a whole experiment on one page, and physics leans on that harder every year. Once slope means velocity and area means displacement, you can read a motion you were never told about — and the same two moves carry straight into acceleration, forces and energy later.

objectives.text: Read velocity off the slope of a position-time graph, including sign.
Tell average velocity and average speed apart, and compute both for a whole trip.
Find acceleration from a velocity-time graph and displacement from the area under it.
State the physical significance of a line of best fit's slope and intercept.
Use a fitted expression in both directions — predict a position, and solve back for a time.

parentNote.text: Built from the HW04 graphs sheet and the Lab 1 constant-motion write-up. Both are graph-heavy and the originals rely on printed graphs I cannot reproduce, so every graph here is drawn fresh by the app with its own numbers — she can work through this and still have both sheets unspoiled. The lab's own questions shape the unit deliberately: predict forward from the expression, solve backwards for the other variable, say what the slope means physically, reason counterfactually about a faster car, and rank slopes where two can tie. That last one is asked as multiple choice over candidate rankings rather than a drag-to-order question, because a put-in-order question cannot express a tie and two of the lines have the same slope. The thing most likely to trip her up is average velocity versus average speed on the out-and-back graph: the trip ends where it started, so average velocity is exactly zero while average speed is not, and both answers are correct at the same time.

nextUp.text: Do the cards first — slope means velocity, area means displacement. The graph questions get much faster once those two are automatic.

cards.def:
**Time on the horizontal axis, position on the vertical.**
• Each point says where the object was at that moment.
• It does not show speed directly — you read speed from the steepness.
cards.hint: A position-time graph is a record of where, not of how fast.

cards.def:
**The slope is the velocity.**
• Rise over run is metres over seconds, which is a speed with a direction attached.
• This is the single most useful fact in the whole topic.
cards.hint: Slope has the units of the answer: m ÷ s = m/s.

cards.def:
**A steeper line on a position–time graph is a faster object.**
• Same time, more ground covered.
• Ranking objects by speed is therefore just ranking lines by steepness — ignoring the sign.
cards.hint: Two lines can lean opposite ways and still be equally fast.

cards.term: Flat line on a position–time graph
cards.def:
**A horizontal line means the object is at rest.**
• Time passes, position does not change, so the slope is zero.
• Zero slope is still a real velocity — it is a velocity of zero.
cards.hint: Flat is not the same as nothing happening. Time is still running.

cards.def:
**A downward line means the object is moving backward.**
• Its position is decreasing, so the velocity is negative.
• Backward means back towards the origin, not slower.
cards.hint: Sign is direction; steepness is speed. Two separate readings.

cards.def:
**Distance is the ground covered; displacement is the change in position.**
• Walk 20 m out and 20 m back: distance 40 m, displacement 0 m.
• Displacement carries a sign; distance never does.
cards.hint: Displacement only cares where you started and where you stopped.

cards.def:
**Total displacement divided by total time.**
• Uses only the first and last positions — the route in between is irrelevant.
• Can be zero even after a long trip, if you end where you began.
cards.hint: Straight line from start to finish, divided by the clock.

cards.def:
**Total distance divided by total time.**
• Counts every metre travelled, in whichever direction.
• Never negative, and never zero unless nothing moved at all.
cards.hint: Average speed is what the odometer says; average velocity is what the map says.

cards.def:
**Time on the horizontal axis, velocity on the vertical.**
• Now the height of the line is the speed, not the position.
• A horizontal line here means constant velocity, not standing still.
cards.hint: Same-looking flat line, completely different meaning. Check the vertical axis label first, every time.

cards.def:
**The slope is the acceleration.**
• Rise over run is now (m/s) ÷ s, which is m/s².
• Sloping up is speeding up; sloping down is slowing down.
cards.hint: Slope always means 'rate of change of the vertical axis'. Change the axis, change the meaning.

cards.def:
**The area under the line is the displacement.**
• Velocity × time = distance, and that product is exactly an area.
• Split the shape into rectangles and triangles and add them up.
cards.hint: Area below the time axis counts as negative displacement.
cards.eq: Δx = area under the v–t curve

cards.def:
**A single straight line drawn to pass as close as possible to all the data points.**
• It does not have to touch any of them.
• Fitting a line is how you get one clean answer out of messy repeated measurements.
cards.hint: Do not connect the dots. Draw the line the dots are scattered around.

cards.term: What the slope meant in the lab
cards.def:
**The slope of the position–time fit is the car's constant velocity.**
• The car was set to run at one steady speed, so the graph came out straight.
• That is what makes the slope meaningful: it is measuring the thing that was held constant.
cards.hint: The lab asks for the physical significance of the slope. The answer is a speed, with units.

cards.def:
**The y-intercept is the position at time zero — where the car started.**
• An intercept of 2 ft means the car was already 2 ft along when timing began.
• A non-zero intercept is not an error; it is a starting line.
cards.hint: Set t = 0 in the expression and whatever is left is the intercept.

cards.def:
**Position = (slope × time) + intercept.**
• Writing the fit as an equation is what lets you use it instead of squinting at the graph.
• Once you have it, you can go forwards or backwards.
cards.hint: It is y = mx + b wearing physics clothes.

cards.def:
**How far your measured value sits from the accepted one, as a percentage.**
• Take the difference, divide by the accepted value, multiply by 100.
• It answers how good, not just how different.
cards.hint: Divide by the ACCEPTED value, not by your own.

cards.def:
**Put a time in, get a position out.**
• Substitute the time and evaluate — one line of arithmetic.
• Watch the units: if the expression is built in seconds, a time in minutes must be converted first.
cards.hint: Predicting beyond your data is allowed here, as long as the motion stays constant.

cards.def:
**Put a position in, solve for the time.**
• Subtract the intercept, then divide by the slope.
• Same equation, rearranged — this is the half people forget to practise.
cards.hint: Undo the equation in reverse order: the +b comes off before the ÷m.

cards.def:
**A faster car makes a steeper line.**
• Its velocity is larger, and velocity is the slope, so the slope goes up.
• The intercept would not change — it started in the same place.
cards.hint: Ask which quantity changed, then ask which graph feature carries it.

cards.def:
**Two different lines can have exactly the same slope.**
• They are parallel, and represent equal velocities from different starting positions.
• A ranking has to be able to say A = C, not just A > C.
cards.hint: Compute every slope before you rank any of them. Parallel is easy to miss by eye.

questions.q: On a position–time graph, what does the slope of the line tell you?
questions.hint: Check the units of rise over run.
steps: Slope is rise over run: the vertical quantity divided by the horizontal one.
Here that is a change in position divided by a change in time.
Metres divided by seconds is m/s, which is a velocity.
Acceleration would need the vertical axis to be velocity instead.

ex.main: **The velocity.** Rise over run is Δx/Δt, whose units are m/s. Reading the units off the axes tells you what any slope means.
ex.tip: Slope always means 'rate of change of whatever is on the vertical axis'.

questions.q: On a velocity–time graph, what does the slope tell you?
questions.hint: Same rule as before — divide the vertical units by the horizontal ones.
steps: The vertical axis is now velocity in m/s and the horizontal is time in s.
Rise over run is therefore (m/s) divided by s.
That gives m/s², the units of acceleration.
Displacement comes from the area under this graph, not from its slope.

ex.main: **The acceleration.** (m/s) ÷ s = m/s². The rule never changes — only the axis does.
ex.tip: Two graphs, two meanings for slope. Always read the vertical axis label first.

questions.q: A horizontal line on a position–time graph means the object is:
questions.hint: If position is not changing, what is the slope?
steps: A horizontal line has zero slope.
On a position–time graph the slope is the velocity.
Zero velocity means the object is not moving.
Constant speed would be a straight line that is sloping, not flat.

ex.main: **At rest.** Time keeps running, the position does not change, so the velocity is zero. Careful: on a VELOCITY–time graph a horizontal line means the opposite — constant speed.
ex.tip: The same shape means different things on the two graphs. That is the trap this topic is built on.

questions.q: What does the area under a velocity–time graph give you?
questions.hint: Multiply the two axis quantities together and see what you get.
steps: An area is a height multiplied by a width.
Here that is velocity multiplied by time.
m/s × s = m, a distance along the axis — a displacement.
So the area under the line is how far the object moved.

ex.main: **The displacement.** Velocity × time is a distance, and that product is exactly what an area is. Area under the axis counts as negative.
ex.tip: Slope and area are the two tools. Slope divides the axes, area multiplies them.

questions.q: In the fitted expression x = vt + x₀, what does x₀ represent?
opts: The percent error in the fit
questions.hint: Substitute t = 0 and see what is left.
steps: Put t = 0 into the expression.
The vt term becomes zero, leaving x = x₀.
So x₀ is the position at the very start of timing.
On the graph it is where the fitted line crosses the vertical axis.

ex.main: **The position when timing began.** It is the y-intercept. A non-zero value is not a mistake — it just means the car was already down the track when the clock started.
ex.tip: To find what any constant means, set the other variable to zero.

questions.q: An object walks 20 m forward and then 20 m back to where it started. What is its displacement?
questions.hint: Displacement compares only the start and the finish.
steps: Displacement is the change in position: final minus initial.
The object finished exactly where it began.
So the change in position is zero.
The 40 m it covered is the distance, which is a different quantity.

ex.main: **0 m.** Displacement asks only where you ended relative to where you started. The 40 m is the distance travelled.
ex.tip: Two questions worth asking separately: how far did it go, and how far is it from home.

questions.q: A line of best fit should be drawn so that it:
opts: Passes exactly through every data point
Passes as close as it can to all points
Connects the first and the last point
questions.hint: What is the point of taking repeated measurements?
steps: Repeated measurements scatter because of small random errors.
A best-fit line represents the trend those scattered points share.
So it is drawn to sit as close as it can to all of them at once.
It may touch none of them, and it is not forced through the origin.

ex.main: **As close as possible to all of them.** Connecting the dots would preserve the noise, which is the opposite of what fitting is for.
ex.tip: If your line hits every point exactly, suspect that you drew the noise instead of the trend.

questions.q: In the graph shown, during which interval is the object moving backward?
questions.hint: Backward means the position is decreasing.
steps: Moving backward means the position value is getting smaller.
From 0 to 10 s the line rises, so the object moves forward.
From 10 to 20 s the line is flat, so it is at rest.
From 20 to 30 s the line falls from 20 m back to 0 m, so that is the backward interval.

ex.main: **From 20 to 30 s.** The line slopes down, so the position is decreasing and the velocity is negative — about −2 m/s.
ex.tip: Read a position–time graph in three passes: rising, flat, falling. Label each before answering anything.

questions.q: For the whole 30-second trip in the graph shown, what is the average velocity?
questions.hint: Average velocity needs only the first and last positions.
steps: Average velocity is total displacement divided by total time.
The object starts at 0 m and finishes at 0 m, so its displacement is 0 m.
Zero divided by 30 s is zero.
The object certainly moved — but it ended where it began, so the average VELOCITY is zero.

ex.main: **0 m/s.** The trip ends at the starting position, so the displacement is zero and so is the average velocity. This is not a trick: it is what the quantity means.
ex.tip: If a graph ends at the same height it started, the average velocity is zero before you calculate anything.

questions.q: An object moves out and then returns, as shown in the graph. What is its average speed for the whole 30-second trip?
questions.hint: Average speed counts every metre covered, in both directions.
steps: Average speed is total distance divided by total time.
Out: 0 m to 20 m is 20 m. Resting: 0 m. Back: 20 m to 0 m is another 20 m.
Total distance is 40 m over 30 s.
40 ÷ 30 = 1.33 m/s. Note the average velocity for this same trip is 0 — both answers are right at once.

ex.main: **1.33 m/s.** Distance adds up regardless of direction, so the return leg counts too. Average speed and average velocity answer different questions about the same journey.
ex.tip: When a question offers 0 alongside a positive value, check which of the two it is asking for.

questions.q: In the velocity–time graph shown, what is the acceleration between 0 and 10 seconds?
questions.hint: Acceleration is the slope of this graph.
steps: Read the two endpoints of that segment: velocity goes from 0 to 20 m/s.
The time taken is 10 s.
Acceleration is the slope: Δv ÷ Δt = 20 ÷ 10.
That gives +2 m/s², positive because the object is speeding up.

ex.main: **2 m/s².** Δv/Δt = 20/10. The 20 on its own is the velocity reached, not the acceleration — the division by time is what makes it a rate.
ex.tip: An option that repeats a number straight off the axis is usually the trap.

questions.q: The constant-motion lab produced the fit x = 0.8t + 2, with x in feet and t in seconds. How far has the car travelled at t = 0.5 minutes?
questions.hint: The expression is built in seconds. What is 0.5 minutes?
steps: The expression uses seconds, so convert first: 0.5 min × 60 = 30 s.
Substitute: x = 0.8(30) + 2.
So the car is at 26 ft. Skipping the conversion and using 0.5 gives 2.4 ft, which is the trap.

ex.main: **26 ft.** The conversion is part of the work, not a formality — substituting 0.5 straight in gives 2.4 ft, off by a factor of sixty.
ex.tip: Before substituting anything, check that its units match the ones the expression was built from.

questions.q: A constant-motion lab gives the fit x = 0.8t + 2, with x in feet and t in seconds. How long does the car take to reach 30 ft?
questions.hint: This one runs the equation backwards. Undo the +2 first.
steps: Set the expression equal to the target position: 30 = 0.8t + 2.
Subtract the intercept from both sides: 28 = 0.8t.
Divide by the slope: t = 28 ÷ 0.8 = 35 s.
Forgetting to subtract the 2 first gives 37.5 s, which is the common slip.

ex.main: **35 s.** Subtract the intercept, then divide by the slope — undo the equation in reverse order.
ex.tip: Predicting a position and solving for a time use the same fit. Practise both directions or only one will be quick.

questions.q: A car's measured velocity is 0.8 ft/s and the accepted value is 0.75 ft/s. What is the percent error?
questions.hint: Divide by the accepted value, not by your own measurement.
steps: Find the difference: 0.80 − 0.75 = 0.05 ft/s.
Divide by the ACCEPTED value: 0.05 ÷ 0.75 = 0.0667.
Multiply by 100 to get 6.7%.
Dividing by the measured 0.80 instead gives 6.3%, which is the usual mistake.

ex.main: **6.7%.** 0.05/0.75 × 100. The accepted value goes on the bottom — that is what the error is being judged against.
ex.tip: When two close answers appear, one of them is usually the same sum with the wrong denominator.

questions.q: Using the velocity–time graph shown, what is the total displacement over the full 40 seconds?
questions.hint: Split the shape into a triangle, a rectangle and another triangle.
steps: Displacement is the area under the line, so break the shape into pieces.
0–10 s is a triangle: ½ × 10 × 20 = 100 m.
10–30 s is a rectangle: 20 × 20 = 400 m.
30–40 s is another triangle: ½ × 10 × 20 = 100 m. Total 100 + 400 + 100 = 600 m.

ex.main: **600 m.** Triangle, rectangle, triangle. Treating the whole shape as a rectangle gives 800 m — the two sloped ends are half-areas, not full ones.
ex.tip: Cut every area problem into rectangles and triangles before you calculate anything.

questions.q: Four cars have straight position–time lines. W passes (0 s, 0 m) and (4 s, 12 m). X passes (0, 0) and (6, 6). Y passes (0, 2) and (5, 17). Z passes (0, 0) and (8, 4). Rank their speeds, greatest first.
questions.hint: Work out all four slopes before ranking. Two of them match.
steps: W: rise 12 over run 4 = 3 m/s.
X: 6 over 6 = 1 m/s. Z: 4 over 8 = 0.5 m/s.
Y: from (0,2) to (5,17) the rise is 15 over a run of 5 = 3 m/s — the different starting position does not change the slope.
So W and Y tie at 3, then X at 1, then Z at 0.5: W = Y > X > Z.

ex.main: **W = Y > X > Z.** Y starts 2 m further along, which shifts its line up but leaves its steepness alone. A ranking has to be able to say 'equals'.
ex.tip: A different intercept never changes a slope. Compute every slope before comparing any of them.

questions.q: In the constant-motion lab, what is the physical significance of the slope of the position–time line, and how would you know?
opts: The car's constant velocity — rise over run has units of ft/s
The distance the car travelled, read off the vertical axis
The time the car took, read off the horizontal axis
The car's acceleration, since the line is straight
questions.hint: Let the units answer the question for you.
steps: Take rise over run for this graph: feet divided by seconds.
ft/s is a speed, so the slope must represent a speed.
The line is straight, which means that speed never changed — the car ran at one constant velocity.
A straight line means zero acceleration, not constant acceleration, so acceleration cannot be what the slope shows.

ex.main: **The car's constant velocity, and the units prove it.** ft ÷ s = ft/s. Straightness tells you the velocity was constant, which is exactly what the lab set out to test.
ex.tip: 'How did you know' questions want the units or the shape as evidence, not just the right noun.

questions.q: In the constant-motion lab, a car released from a starting mark gives the position–time line shown. If the lab were repeated with a faster car released from that same mark, how would the graph change?
opts: Steeper line and a higher y-intercept
questions.hint: Name the quantity that changed, then ask which feature of the graph carries it.
steps: Identify what changed between the two runs: only the car's speed.
On a position–time graph the velocity is carried by the slope, so a faster car gives a steeper line.
The starting mark is unchanged, and the starting position is the y-intercept, so the intercept stays put.
The speed is still constant, so the line stays straight rather than curving.

ex.main: **Steeper, same intercept.** Faster means a bigger slope; same starting mark means the same intercept. A curve would mean the speed was changing, which it is not.
ex.tip: For any 'what if' question, name the changed quantity first, then the graph feature that carries it.

questions.q: An object's position–time graph is a straight line sloping downward. What does its velocity–time graph look like?
opts: A horizontal line below the time axis
A horizontal line above the time axis
A line starting high and crossing to negative
questions.hint: Straight on a position graph means the velocity is constant. What sign is it?
steps: A straight position–time line has a constant slope, so the velocity is constant.
Constant velocity plots as a horizontal line on a velocity–time graph.
The position line slopes downward, so that constant velocity is negative.
A negative constant plots as a horizontal line below the time axis.

ex.main: **A horizontal line below the axis.** Straight position line → constant velocity → horizontal on the v–t graph; downward slope → that constant is negative.
ex.tip: Translate in two steps: straight-or-curved decides the shape, up-or-down decides the sign.

questions.q: Two objects cover the same distance in the same time, but one has a positive velocity and the other negative. What can you say about their speeds and their position–time lines?
opts: Equal speeds; lines equally steep, sloping opposite
Different speeds; one line is steeper than the other
Equal speeds; the two lines are exactly identical
One is at rest, since the velocities cancel out
questions.hint: Steepness and sign are two separate readings of the same line.
steps: Speed is the size of the velocity, ignoring its sign.
Same distance in the same time means the sizes are equal, so the speeds are equal.
Steepness on a position–time graph carries that size, so both lines are equally steep.
The signs differ, so one slopes up and the other slopes down — mirror images, not identical.

ex.main: **Equal speeds, mirrored lines.** Steepness carries the speed and sign carries the direction; reading them separately answers the question in one step.
ex.tip: Velocities cancelling is about adding two motions together. Here there are two separate objects, so nothing cancels.

questions.q: For the velocity–time graph shown, what is the average velocity across the whole 40 seconds?
questions.hint: You already know the displacement from the area. Now divide.
steps: Average velocity is total displacement divided by total time.
Displacement is the area under the line: a triangle, a rectangle, then a triangle.
Divide by the 40 s total: 600 ÷ 40 = 15 m/s, which sits below the 20 m/s cruising speed as it must.

ex.main: **15 m/s.** Area gives 600 m, then divide by 40 s. It has to come out below the 20 m/s cruising speed, which is a useful check on the answer.
ex.tip: Sanity-check an average against the range it must fall inside. Anything above the peak is wrong on sight.

sorts.title: Which graph is it true of?

items.t: The slope of the line is the object's velocity
items.why: Rise is position, run is time, so slope is position over time — velocity.

items.t: A flat horizontal line means the object is at rest
items.why: Position not changing over time is standing still.

items.t: A line sloping downward means the object is moving backward
items.why: Position decreasing over time — heading back toward the origin.

items.t: A steeper line means a faster object
items.why: More position covered per second is a bigger velocity.

items.t: The y-intercept is where the object started
items.why: At time zero the graph reads the starting position.

items.t: The slope of the line is the acceleration
items.why: Rise is velocity, run is time — velocity over time is acceleration.

items.t: The area under the line is the displacement
items.why: Velocity × time is displacement, and that product is the area under the line.

items.t: A flat horizontal line means constant velocity
items.why: Velocity not changing over time is constant velocity — the object is still moving.

items.t: The line crossing the time axis means the object turned around
items.why: Velocity passing through zero and changing sign is a change of direction.

items.t: A steeper line means the velocity is changing faster
items.why: More velocity gained per second is a bigger acceleration.
